speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Singapore is one of the safest countries in the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is, in large part, due to the Singapore Police Force, or SPF in short.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill seeks to amend the Police Force Act, or PFA, so that SPF can carry out its mission to prevent, deter and detect crime and ensure the safety and security of Singaporeans even more effectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill enhances the regime against evading Police roadblocks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Drivers who evade roadblocks endanger the lives of Police officers and other road users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In an ensuing car chase, for example, evading drivers often exhibit dangerous driving behaviours, such as speeding, running red lights and swerving in and out of lanes suddenly without warning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In 2017, a driver was instructed to stop at a roadblock.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Not only did he not stop his vehicle, he dashed through the roadblock, which triggered a chase.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: He was sentenced to only three weeks' imprisonment for the offence of roadblock evasion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We were lucky that the driver did not cause harm in that instance to other road users and to our officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In other instances, roadblock evasion has led to more serious damage to property and even injuries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 6 will also expand the definition of roadblock evasion to cover more modalities of evasion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Currently, the offence of roadblock evasion only applies to drivers who physically dash through a roadblock with their vehicle.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, SPF has encountered cases where drivers evade roadblocks by other ways, such as reversing, making a U-turn or alighting from their vehicle and escaping on foot.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In 2016, a motorcyclist stopped before a roadblock, abandoned his vehicle and fled on foot.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While arresting the motorcyclist, a Police officer was injured.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The motorcyclist was, eventually, convicted of voluntarily causing hurt to a public servant, unlawful possession of a weapon and possession of a controlled drug.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, no further action could be taken against him for evading the roadblock, as he did not physically dash through it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 6 will make it an offence for a driver to fail to follow a Police officer's order, be it given by a spoken word, a hand signal, a notice or a sign, warning of the presence of a roadblock, to proceed towards a roadblock, stop, remain in the vehicle and keep the vehicle stationary until he or she is permitted to proceed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, on the set-up of barriers to control human traffic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: SPF sets up various types of barriers to control human traffic, such as to prevent members of the public from entering a crime scene or high-security area.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, even though the PFA provides that SPF has the duty to take lawful measures to preserve public peace and prevent and detect crimes and offences, the PFA does not explicitly empower Police officers to set up these barriers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 6 makes explicit Police officers' powers to erect barriers to control human traffic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It also creates an offence for persons who fail to follow a Police officer's order to not cross such barriers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, forced entry for cases of medical emergency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Police officers' powers to make forced entry are currently scoped to very specific circumstances, such as to perform rescue operations in cases of attempted suicide or to arrest suspects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, Police officers would sometimes also respond to cases of medical emergency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In June 2021, SPF received a call from a resident who heard a weak voice coming from a nearby unit asking for help.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: A senior resident resided in that unit alone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: When our officers arrived outside the unit, they could not hear any sounds, were unable to contact the senior or even his next-of-kin and were told by his neighbour that the senior had just returned home from the hospital that very morning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As the senior could have been in dire need of help, the Police officers decided to make a forced entry immediately.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: They discovered that the senior had fallen and was unable to move.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Thanks to our officers' actions, the senior was able to receive help quickly and was conveyed to the hospital.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Currently, in such cases of medical emergency, Police officers rely on the common law defence of necessity to make forced entry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, on providing Special Police Officers, or SPOs, with the same powers conferred on regular Police officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: SPOs comprise four categories of officers – full-time Police National Servicemen, or NSmen; Operationally-ready Police NSmen; Volunteer Ex-NSmen; and Volunteer Special Constabulary Officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In the PFA, our SPOs are vested with the same duties as regular Police officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Like regulars, they have the duty to prevent and detect crimes, preserve public peace and protect persons from injury or death.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, SPOs, currently, only have powers of investigation under Part IV of the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC).

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This means that while they have the power to arrest a suspect or execute a search warrant, they do not have powers beyond investigations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These include the powers to set up roadblocks and search a person before they enter a high-security area.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This will allow SPF to deploy SPOs to a wider range of operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To ensure that these powers are exercised appropriately, SPF has in place robust safeguards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: SPF will ensure that only SPOs who pass the requisite training can exercise policing powers and be deployed on the frontline.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: SPOs who are deemed unsuitable to exercise policing powers will be deployed to perform backend and administrative duties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For those who misuse their powers, SPF will take strict disciplinary action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In serious cases, we will also initiate criminal proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, providing Commercial Affairs Officers, or CAOs, with necessary powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: CAOs are public officers employed by SPF to investigate commercial and financial crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Currently, the PFA only provides CAOs with the powers of investigation under Part IV of the CPC.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, there are other powers which are necessary for their work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, CAOs, currently, have the power to arrest suspects for an arrestable offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There will be safeguards to prevent CAOs from misusing their new powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 9 makes it explicit that CAOs are subject to certain restrictions when carrying out procedures relating to arrest and search, such as the mode for searching women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These are the same restrictions which apply to Police officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: CAOs must also attend training and pass the requisite tests before they can exercise these powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, empowering the Commissioner of Police to delegate his powers to civilian officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Currently, the Commissioner can delegate his powers to Police officers in leadership positions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, he cannot do the same for civilian officers in leadership positions, such as the Director of the Commercial Affairs Department (CAD).

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, if the CAD Director wishes to issue Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) on how to handle cases of specific commercial crimes to Investigation Officers, he will have to ask a Police officer to do so on his behalf.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Some powers conferred on the Commissioner will continue to be non-delegable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Examples include those under the Public Order and Safety (Special Powers) Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, protecting officers from liability for acts done in good faith and with reasonable care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: At times, Police officers have to make split-second decisions and take decisive action in order to save lives, even if their actions may result in injury or damage to property.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Such time-critical and dangerous situations are often a matter of life and death and present themselves in high-stress environments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, if a patrolling Police officer finds a person in a crowded public place waving around a chopper in his hand and shouting at passers-by and, if the person becomes increasingly agitated, the Police officer might tase the person to ensure public safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Here, the defence of good faith and reasonable care applies even if the person suffers injuries as a result, as the Police officer believed honestly and based on objectively reasonable grounds that his actions were necessary to prevent harm and the Police officer had adhered to the standard operating protocol for using a taser to restrain a dangerous and armed person.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: When carrying out their lawful duties, our officers can already rely on the common law defence of necessity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But we want to give greater assurance to our officers and make it explicit that they have protection for acts done in good faith and with reasonable care under the law, so that they can carry out their duties with greater confidence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is similar to the protection that is already accorded to other Home Team officers, such as SCDF officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It only applies when our officers have acted in good faith and with reasonable care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Officers who act irresponsibly will be subjected to disciplinary proceedings or even criminal proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, the Bill provides SPF with the legal power to retain the employment of regular Police Officers during a major crisis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Major crises may include a major terrorist incident or a large-scale, sustained public order incident.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: SPF would need to have sufficient manpower to manage such crises.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Today, SPF can already mobilise SPOs under certain circumstances and require them to serve until they are demobilised.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Full-time NSmen and Operationally-ready NSmen can already be retained for mobilised service upon a proclamation by the President under section 16 of the Enlistment Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For volunteers, the Commissioner of Police can already mobilise them for active service under any circumstances under section 73 of the PFA, so long as the Minister’s permission is sought.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, SPF does not have the legal power to stop regular Police Officers from resigning in the midst of a major crisis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Commissioner must be of the opinion that the officer’s service is necessary for the securing of the public safety, defence and security of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The definition of a “crisis” only applies when the President has issued a Proclamation of Emergency under the Constitution, or the Minister for Home Affairs has given an activation order under the Public Order and Safety (Special Powers) Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is broadly similar to how the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) can already retain regular servicemen for mobilised service upon a proclamation by the President pursuant to section 16 of the Enlistment Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I will now speak about the second objective to improve SPF's disciplinary, administrative and human resources processes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This ensures our officers continue to uphold the highest standards of integrity and conduct.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, today, SPF issues recall orders under the Enlistment Act to compel NSmen to report for disciplinary proceedings and NSmen can claim for loss in civilian remuneration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 16 allows SPF to issue orders under the PFA to compel NSmen who have committed disciplinary offences to report for disciplinary proceedings without having to make up for any loss in civilian remuneration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is because the disciplinary proceedings arose out of their own wrongful actions in the first place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Similar provisions for SCDF and SAF NSmen already exist in the Civil Defence Act and the Singapore Armed Forces Act respectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, currently, the Commissioner’s approval has to be sought for the discharge of NSFs for reasons other than completing full-time service, even when the reasons are straightforward, such as the NSF having a serious medical condition or being transferred to the SAF or SCDF.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To streamline this process, clause 13 specifies the conditions under which NSFs may be discharged from SPF automatically, without the need for the Commissioner’s approval.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This aligns with the approach for Operationally-ready NSmen, who can already be automatically discharged under the same conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, currently, the PFA allows the Minister to make regulations for Police associations, such as the Police Central Welfare Fund, which advance the welfare of regular Police officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 28 allows the Minister to also include SPOs and civilian officers employed by SPF in Police associations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is in recognition of the contributions that they make to support SPF in ensuring the safety and security of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Currently, full-time NSmen and Operationally-ready NSmen in SPF serve in one of two Forces: they may serve in the Special Constabulary, where they perform the same duties as regular Police officers and have powers of investigation under Part IV of the CPC.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Otherwise, they may also serve in the Vigilante Corps.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Since the introduction of the VC in 1964, VC officers have made important contributions in supporting SPF to maintain law and order in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: They mainly perform support roles and do not have any policing powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This gives our NSmen the opportunity to be deployed in a greater variety of roles in SPF.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill also makes minor amendments to streamline SPF’s administrative and human resources, which I will not go into further here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill also strengthens controls over Auxiliary Police Forces (APFs), which provide armed security services and supplement the Home Team’s efforts in ensuring the safety and security of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The armed security industry was liberalised in 2004 to allow more APFs to operate islandwide.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This was in consideration of the increasingly complex security environment, which required a larger pool of armed officers to step up security measures at various critical infrastructure and key installations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: With the APFs providing support for such functions, SPF is also better able to focus on its core mission to prevent, deter and detect crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We had stated then that it was necessary to ensure that only trusted agents may operate and manage APFs in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These considerations remain valid today, as Auxiliary Police Officers bear arms and are vested with certain powers to perform their functions effectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: They also have access to the sensitive locations where they are deployed to protect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Having reviewed the regulatory regimes of other essential services sectors and the prevailing operating environment, we felt that we should update the APF controls in the PFA, to ensure that the controls remain effective.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Currently, the PFA requires an APF employer to obtain the Minister’s approval before the APF employer is acquired by any other person.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Minister’s approval is also required before one becomes a substantial shareholder of an APF employer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Going forward, we will make these controls more holistic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These thresholds, which take reference from the legislation of other essential services sectors, ensure that only trusted agents can have the ability to influence and direct actions of the APF.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 19 imposes a requirement on APF employers to inform the Commissioner after becoming aware of such transactions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This provides another layer to detect any potential attempts to circumvent our reporting and approval requirements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There may be circumstances, such as public emergencies, where it is crucial that we ensure the continuity of security services provided by the APFs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This regime is found in other essential services sectors, to ensure no disruptions to the provision of these services.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We move on with the Second Reading for the Police Force (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill marks another important step ahead in protecting the safety and security of Singaporeans and enforcement officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is perhaps also most opportune during the 200th year of the establishment of the Singapore Police Force (SPF).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The enhancement of the SPF’s operational capabilities is greatly welcomed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Officers must be assured that they are protected so that they can discharge their duties without the nagging worries of personal liability while legitimately carrying out their duties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We note that this has been carefully calibrated: greater protection is afforded to our officers but balanced by criminal liability and disciplinary actions to prevent and punish those who flagrantly abuse their powers in bad faith.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our officers do not operate in a risk-free, benign and simplistic environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They often have to rely on their training, exercise judgement and take on certain risks, especially in critical, complex and time-sensitive situations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In my years of running operations in the Police Force, I have seen that even the best officers could and would make mistakes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And these mistakes were crucial to the Police's collective learning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mistakes can also come from taking well-managed risks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Nothing affects the ability of an officer to discharge his duties more than knowing that the law does not protect them or is even against them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that these considerations can be included in the upcoming regulations to be prescribed by the Ministry in determining what constitutes "good faith" and "reasonable care".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These regulations should also not be unnecessarily rigid or prescriptive such that they stifles execution in fluid operational situations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, neither could it be so broad as to leave practitioners directionless.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister share what might some of these regulations be?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What were examples of cases that the officers did not act in good faith or reasonable care?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Enforcement officers work in a hierarchy with clear chains of command.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are usually either guided by supervisors or Standard Operating Procedures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If there is, indeed, a situation where an officer did not act in good faith and/or reasonable care, then what is also the liability of officers in the chain of command?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that officers do not lose operational effectiveness in becoming overly circumspect in guiding their officers or executing their duties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: My first suggestion relates to motorists who evade road barriers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Mackenzie Road incident in 2017, which left two of our officers injured, has shown us how brazen a minority of motorists can be in evading road barriers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Evasion not only reflects intent to conceal criminality but can also cause considerable danger and inconvenience.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe this would serve as a forceful deterrent, demonstrating the Ministry's zero-tolerance stance towards such acts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At present, liability under section 87(9) is not explicit within the following provisions: sections 87(5), (7) and (8).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These subsections are important in ensuring that the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) retains regulatory oversight over how APFs are run.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, section 87(7) underlines the need for Singaporeans to retain the controlling interests in APF companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Should we attach legal liabilities for infringing the above-mentioned provisions?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can I also clarify that section 88 also applies to entities and persons with indirect control over the board of the employer of the Auxiliary Police Forces?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, company A has an indirect control over the employer of the APF via a controlling stake in the parent company owning the employer of the APFs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Ultimately, the Ministry should be afforded greater regulatory oversight over APFs, ensuring that APFs maintain the highest standards expected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our officers must be provided with the full armour of the law to take the stand against criminals and discharge their duties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the delegation of powers to civilian officers; second, the conduct of roadblocks; and third, the new powers to be given to Commercial Affairs Officers and Special Police Officers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the existing Act, the powers of the Commissioner (CP) may be delegated by him to a Police officer not below the rank of superintendent.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the case of the Deputy Commissioner (DCP), his powers may be delegated by CP to a Police officer not below the rank of an assistant superintendent.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the Ministry's media release on the Bill on 5 July, it was clarified that this provision would allow delegation of CP’s or DCP’s powers to civilian officers in leadership positions within the SPF.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am somewhat concerned about what this change will entail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, is it envisaged that the command of the force at the highest levels could conceivably be delegated to civilian officers from time to time?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If this is so, I wonder how well this will go down amongst uniformed officers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Further, developing Police leadership skills is a specialised field that, in recent years, has been spearheaded by the Police Psychological Services Division.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The assessments require potential Police leaders to be put through simulations of incident management at the frontline and officers are also continually developed for Police leadership.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is also an organisational culture amongst uniformed personnel which can be quite distinct from civilians working in the same organisation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That being the case, one has to wonder about the delegation of Police leadership powers at the highest level to civilians.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While these civilians may be senior enough in grade, would they have the necessary experience and credibility to exercise such command responsibilities?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Although there are other provisions in the main Act that allow for assignment of powers to civilians, they are usually clearly scoped.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, section 18 of the Act enables the Minister to appoint civilians to exercise powers to grant licences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To expect civilians to exercise such administrative powers seems unobjectionable, compared with the prospect of them exercising command or frontline powers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A further explanation of what is envisaged would be necessary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier in the Second Reading speech, the Minister of State did reiterate or confirm that certain powers of the CP would be non-delegable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Where are we to find this list for clarification?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the amendments, it is much more explicit what drivers and Police officers can and cannot do.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This sub-section will make it an offence for pedestrians travelling in the direction of a roadblock to cross the barrier and subjects pedestrians to the officers’ instructions as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, the Minister of State explained that one of the targets for this provision are car drivers who attempt to abandon their cars and escape on foot.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could he clarify whether there are other categories of pedestrians who are being envisioned by this new provision?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From my understanding, CAD has had Police officers attached to it since it was formed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This arrangement was made precisely because the CAO’s powers were limited; when it was time to do raids, the Police officers attached to CAD would accompany the investigators in charge to exercise their full powers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My understanding is that this arrangement has worked for many years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is this due to manpower shortage issues or some other operational reason?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: On the whole, I do support the Bill.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, there are certain queries or concerns I have which I will put forth.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, the Commissioner may only delegate his and the Deputy Commissioner's powers to Police officers in leadership positions within SPF.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Non-Police personnel may not have the same experiences as a Police officer.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I would like to clarify in what instances the Minister of State envisages the need to execute section 17.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I feel this is especially pertinent and important in domestic violence cases where the victim may be in imminent danger.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Having this amendment will add another layer of protection to the victims as it allows the Police officers to render help immediately as time may be of the essence in such cases.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would still call for caution when executing forced entry.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There should be clear guidelines on what is considered a reasonable situation for it and all officers should be suitably trained before being able to exercise these powers.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This may be particularly important in domestic violence cases where it is not clear or easy to determine if a crime is being committed in the premises.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, in cases of forced entry, there may be circumstances in which there may be damage to the premises, or instances when the forced entry is actually unwarranted.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, like to clarify if there is proper recourse available to the premise owner in such cases.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, I welcome the fact that forced entry is not applicable to persons who may be attempting suicide.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I do agree that these are very complex and, possibly, emotionally-charged situations.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Officers who do not understand the ramifications of forcing entry into premises occupied by a suicidal person may run the risk of making matters worse.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The person they are trying to help may end up seriously injured or dead, with the officer as a contributing factor, intentionally or otherwise.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And if they do have the requisite powers, what sort of legal protections are afforded to them in the event their actions lead to undesirable consequences for the suicidal individual?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, for section 120A, which relates to the granting of permission for the sale or manufacture of Police uniform or insignia, may I suggest that the word "written" be inserted before the word "permission" in the revised section, meaning the section should be amended to read, "has the written permission of the Commissioner" for clarity and transparency of procedure?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Before ending, I would also like to congratulate the Singapore Police Force on celebrating their 200th Anniversary.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: May they continue their good work for many more years to come.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I strongly support the empowerment of our officers in order to achieve more efficient response to emergencies and assist people in distress.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This measure will help to save lives and prevent tragedies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have been concerned about the safety of Police officers on duty at roadblocks which are necessary to deter drink-driving, illegally-modified vehicles and associated offences.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the empowerment of the APFs be helpful in supporting more roadblock operations at problematic road segments?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am referring to those which many residents provide feedback about, particularly speeding and noisy modified vehicles.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry consider allowing APFs to carry out such operations independently so as to achieve a greater deterrent effect?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, will the Police look into more transportable and solid barriers to minimise the risk to the lives of the Police on duty at roadblocks and to deter dash-throughs, such as by putting up impact absorbers used by contractors on highways while carrying out construction works?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will such operations be effective against motorcyclists who have more avenues to evade the roadblocks?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to ask if the Police will equip all the staff and officers, including SPOs and CAOs, with cameras and recorders.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The records should be kept independently for safekeeping as evidence to prevent wrongful accusations and misuse.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such information shall not be shared, unless with permission and when needed to respond to fake news and wrongful accusations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Safeguarding of these recordings is also necessary to prevent cyberattacks and manipulation that could jeopardise the safety of operations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While SPF is provided with the power to retain the services of Police officers in times of crises, it should also be provided with an alternative for such officers to be redeployed to other appropriate services.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is because commitment and dedication are required to maintain the integrity and efficiency of operations during a crises.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Officers should be able to address an appeal board for reviews of their cases.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I would also like to take this opportunity to thank the Police Force for keeping Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I will cover three areas as regards these provisions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The first is the provisions to do with tightening control over the controllers of APFs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The second is with regards to advertising for security services by APFs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The third is the introduction of a special administrative order or other order that the Minister may make under certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Our APFs are an extension of the Singapore Police Force and it is critical to ensure that there is accountability to the Minister for Home Affairs as regards control, so as to ensure that our APFs are not diverted from their missions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is an important new section, which also provides sufficiently heavy penalties for offenders.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On this particular amendment, Sir, I have a point of clarification.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Some of our APFs, like Certis and AETOS are both employers of armed APFs and owners of security agencies that carry out unarmed services, but which bear their same logo and same name.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, APFs must exercise caution in how they advertise and hold out their non-APF businesses in such manner that there is no conflation between their APF business and non-APF business.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: MHA and the Commissioner may wish to consider how to ensure this, perhaps through the promulgation of guidelines or further regulations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This new proviso ensures that the provision of essential security services remains unhindered and coordinated across employers of APFs, especially in view of the central role that our APFs have played in our COVID-19 response, which I will elaborate on.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These services included administration of quarantine orders to Persons under Quarantine (PUQs) and the enforcement of such orders as directed by MOH.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In a recent article in June 2021 by Yahoo, several persons affected by such orders described the effort as "disorganised" and officers as "unhelpful" and who caused frustration and confusion amidst PUQs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I thus urge Singaporeans to be empathetic when interacting with our officers as they go about carrying out their duties in this regard.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I was also happy to read in that same Yahoo article that MOH acknowledged the concerns raised and said it would continue to improve communications between the various agencies involved, including Certis.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Alongside Certis, AETOS and SATS, APOs also stepped up in our battle against COVID-19, being deployed at various locations across the island, including Government quarantine facilities, floating hotels under the Maritime and Port Authority, airports, military camps and high-risk areas like the red migrant worker dormitories last year.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Such high-risk locations meant that officers had to don full personal protective equipment for their entire 12-hour shifts, as they assisted with temperature checks, social distancing measures and escorting workers who had tested positive.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They are part of the private security industry and have been situated on the frontlines, engaging in traffic and crowd control, event security, providing remote surveillance and enforcing security rules and regulations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, they are strategically relied on to provide protective security for many important and sensitive Government and civilian institutions, such as at our airports, naval installations and checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While some APFs provide extremely specialised services, as private entities, they are freed from various obligations and restrictions and can operate flexibly and competitively.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is precisely why, Sir, it is extremely important that we ensure that there are sufficient controls over the employers of APFs or the controllers of APFs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In December last year, an APO was headbutted several times by a member of the public.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In January this year, another APO was punched on the head while carrying out safe distancing checks.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened that swift action was taken and, appropriately, heavy punishment meted out.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, Sir, I would also like to take this opportunity to express my gratitude to all our APOs for carrying out their duties diligently and professionally during this pandemic and, even before that, to keep Singapore secure and orderly.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I trust we will see our APOs and, for that matter, our security officers, increasingly not just as partners of the Home Team but as part of the Home Team.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Due to their professionalism and hard work over the decades, our APFs and APOs are respected and trusted by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, today's amendments to strengthen control over the APFs to ensure their continued operations as going concerns and that they stay true to their mission are timely and welcomed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I also welcome the other amendments that strengthen our Police Force.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The amendments will enable SPF to continue keeping Singapore safe and secure amidst an increasingly complex operating environment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I would like to raise three clarifications: One, more clarity on the power to enter any place in case of an emergency; two, the delegation of Commissioner of Police (CP) and Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP) powers; and three, protecting officers from liability for acts done in good faith.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As such, it is appropriate that we do allow our Police officers to enter any place, in case of medical emergency, to protect persons from injury or death.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would allow our Police officers the necessary access in situations where lives may be at stake.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And how would a Police officer assess the medical emergency behind locked doors?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In his opening statement, Minister of State Desmond Tan had shared that one instance in which the CP may consider delegating his power is when the CP delegates his or her power to the Director of Commercial Affairs to issue SOPs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Minister clarify on the type of powers which the CP cannot delegate to civilian officers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will the CP or DCP delegate the power to investigate scams, financial or cybercrimes, given the increase in the number of such crimes which may require a different skillset from the traditional policing?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we have a shortage of this skillset within our current men in blue and how do we ensure that delegating these powers do not dilute the investigative capability of our Police from solving scams, financial or cybercrimes that are getting increasingly complicated?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will allow them to carry out their lawful duties with greater assurance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Nevertheless, officers may still be taken to task and face disciplinary actions or even charged for criminal offences if they are found to have acted inappropriately.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the recent false allegations on social media against our Police Force in the recent months, it underscores the importance of protecting our men in blue in the course of their duty.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: An officer, for example, who has been dispatched to a road traffic accident and is the first officer at the scene, has only a split second to decide on what to do next.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While awaiting the arrival of paramedics, the officer, having been trained in CPR, may need to provide first-aid to the victim.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While administering CPR and trying to resuscitate the victim through chest compressions, the officer may have cracked the victim's ribs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The victim may or may not have survived, but should we not protect our officer for acting in good faith and using as much care as he possibly could at that moment?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The last few weeks also saw an example where a shirtless man was acting aggressively towards our Police officers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The officers were unable to calm the man down, he continued to behave aggressively and, finally, tried to attack our officers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At that point, there was no other option for our officers but to tase the person.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What if the individual who was tased had died due to a pre-existing medical condition?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should the officer not be protected from liability?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It stands to reason that if the officer had acted in good faith and followed all the rules of engagement and SOPs, he should not be personally liable in these instances.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This amendment would undoubtedly protect and reassure our Police officers as they go about their duties.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should this assurance be extended to our Prison wardens and other officers in the Home Team, too?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   It is important for us to equip our Police officers with the necessary powers so that they can respond swiftly in order to protect and save lives.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As such, it is appropriate that we do allow Police officers to enter any place in case of medical emergencies, to protect persons from injury or death.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And how would a Police officer assess the medical emergency behind locked doors?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This amendment also seeks to protect Police officers from liability for acts and omissions done in good faith.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will allow our officers to carry out their duties with greater assurance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the recent false allegations on social media in the recent months against our Police force, it underscores the importance of protecting our Police officers in the course of their duty.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, an officer who has been dispatched to a road traffic accident has only a split second to decide on what to do next.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While waiting for the arrival of paramedics, the officer may need to provide first aid to the victim.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While administering CPR, the officer may have cracked the victim’s ribs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can this assurance be extended to prison wardens and other officers in the Home Team, too?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These officers should be fined and disciplined or prosecuted for criminal offences.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If they are found to have acted inappropriately, they should face stiffer penalties.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Allow me to conclude in English, Sir.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They will honour the contributions of SPF and its officers for keeping Singapore one of the safest countries in the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, I wish to commend SPF for not only keeping our country safe but also for taking steps to make their investigations a fairer process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I previously spoke up to support the video-recording of Police interviews.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad SPF is making efforts to ensure its investigations provide due process to those interviewed by the Police.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is about equipping Police with life-saving skills.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is similar to the powers the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) officers currently have under the Civil Defence Act to break into any place to protect the life, health or safety of individuals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Providing the powers of forced entry gives the officers access to the individual in need of assistance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, just as important is equipping the officer with the skills to provide the assistance required.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: SCDF has a clear mandate to protect life, health and safety and its officers are appropriately trained.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share if Police officers are already receiving training or will receive training to equip them with the skills needed to protect life, health or safety, once they have gained entry?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is about preparing Police officers to appropriately use their new powers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, it gives Special Police Officers the same powers as regular Police officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It gives Commercial Affairs Officers who currently only have investigation powers more powers, such as the power to arrest persons who possess stolen items.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, a Police officer's powers also come with specific safeguards, including requirements and restrictions under the Criminal Procedure Code and Police General Orders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State confirm that the new powers given to Special Police Officers and Commercial Affairs Officers also mean that all the accompanying safeguards apply to them?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State also share what plans there are to provide training for Special Police Officers and Commercial Affairs Officers on their new powers and their accompanying safeguards?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is about maintaining proper staffing during a crisis period.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that in times of crisis, it may be important to retain the services of Police officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But does it make sense to have Police officers stay in the force when they have clearly indicated their unwillingness to do so?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is there a risk that uncommitted Police officers hinder rather than help their comrades during times of crisis?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, can the Minister of State share what plans he has to ensure that the SPF will be adequately staffed to withstand times of crisis, apart from forcing uncommitted Police officers to stay?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The proposed amendments to enhance SPF's operational capabilities and readiness are, therefore, timely as they will enable the Force to better keep Singapore and Singaporeans safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My speech today seeks to gain clarity on why we are increasing the penalties for evading roadblocks and to better understand the rationale for increasing the Police powers for some of our civilian officers, and whether we can better deploy our Police National Service personnel.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While I understand that the new penalties take reference from the offence of voluntarily causing hurt to deter a public servant from his duties, this is a seven-times increase in maximum jail term.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How many cases of drivers evading a police roadblock have been recorded in the past five years?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Are we seeing a significant upward trend, which has necessitated this sharp increase in penalties to send a deterrent message?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How many incidents of roadblock evasion have left our Police officers seriously injured?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A scan through our mainstream media articles found that the last publicised case of Police officers injured by a person evading a roadblock was in June 2017 when Lianhe Wanbao reported that a driver had dashed through a roadblock and injured two Police officers in a violent struggle when being arrested.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This could be the same case cited by the Minister of State yesterday in his opening speech.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In the event where the actions of the driver result in injury, the Police could consider and would probably have done so in the past to serve a charge of voluntarily causing hurt to deter a public servant from his duty or voluntarily causing grievous hurt if the injuries are serious.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Is it, therefore, necessary to raise the penalties for evading a roadblock by seven times?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Next, I would like to better understand the need to confer more Police powers to civilian Commercial Affairs Officers (CAOs).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I was the primary staff officer who coordinated the reconstitution of the Commercial Affairs Department to become a part of the Singapore Police Force back in 2000.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In the process, I helped to put up the paper to establish the CAO scheme of service.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: CAOs are meant to be specialists who perform an important role in combating white collar crime and their good work is vital in helping to maintain Singapore's status as the region's premier financial and commercial hub.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: When establishing the CAO scheme, we knew that we had to look beyond the profile of typical Police officers and attract local talents in law, finance and economics to fight the ever-evolving complex financial crimes ranging from investment and securities fraud to transnational scams.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: CAOs are civilian officers, not Police officers, and there were reasons why they were given only certain Police powers restricted to investigating offences under the Criminal Procedure Code when the CAO scheme was first established.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These were deemed then to be sufficient for the CAOs to carry out their investigation duties effectively, supported by trained and armed Police colleagues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With this amendment, will CAOs be deemed as Police officers henceforth?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The additional powers also come with increased risks.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Would CAOs need to be armed to protect themselves?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To exercise the power of arrest, should we require CAOs to learn defence tactics and pass a yearly Individual Physical Proficiency Test (IPPT), much like what regular Police officers are required to do today?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Would a CAO candidate's Physical Employment Standards (PES) status be now factored into the hiring process?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We established the CAO scheme in 2000 to attract a special group of individuals to join the Police to fight complex white-collar crime.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I recall we started with around 30 CAOs back in 2000.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I believe the number would have grown over the past 20 years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But is that number sufficient to sustain the scheme of service?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What is the attrition rate of CAOs, especially in their first three years of service?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Rather than mould civilian CAOs into pseudo-Police officers, why not consider posting trained, experienced Police officers with the requisite law, finance and economics backgrounds to the Commercial Affairs Department to supplement its current investigative resources?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I strongly believe the Force has today many qualified uniformed men and women capable of handling white-collar crime investigations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I support this and I have a few suggestions on how we could better empower them so that they have a fulfilling time serving their National Service obligation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: During my time in the Force, I observed that PNSFs and PNSmen were more motivated when deployed to perform tasks that were relevant and related to either their area of study or their work experience.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond expanding their powers as proposed in the Bill, can we create a more structured deployment scheme to better leverage the talents of both our PNSFs and PNSmen?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We can and should also better deploy our PNSFs and PNSmen to maximise their fullest potential because every Police officer matters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Please allow me to address their questions in turn.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked if the enhanced regime against roadblock evasion will apply to motorcyclists.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The enhanced regime applies to all modalities of roadblock evasion and will cover all types of vehicles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Gan also asked how many roadblocks were conducted in the past five years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Gan and Mr Melvin Yong also asked how many cases of roadblock evasion were detected, resulted in serious injuries for Police officers, and whether it is necessary to raise the penalties for roadblock evasion when the offender can be charged for other offences like voluntarily causing hurt when their actions result in injury.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Motorists who deliberately evade roadblocks seriously endanger the lives of the Police officers as well as other road users in the vicinity of the roadblock.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In instances where hurt is caused to Police officers, it is true that we can take action using general application provisions like voluntarily causing hurt to deter a public servant from his duty, or voluntarily causing grievous hurt.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, the action of roadblock evasion, by itself, is a serious and risky behaviour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We should not rely on the offender also committing other offences to be able to take the person to task.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Desmond Choo suggested to introduce a mandatory minimum jail sentence for the offence of roadblock evasion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We agree with Mr Choo that motorists who evade roadblocks not only obstruct the course of justice, but also show disregard for the safety of other road users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: That said, we reserve mandatory minimum jail sentences for the most egregious offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For driving-related offences, those that attract mandatory minimum jail sentences are dangerous driving causing death or grievous hurt.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While we agree with Mr Choo that evasion of roadblock can result in dire consequences, we do not think it warrants mandatory minimum jail sentences, at least for now.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We will monitor the situation after the increase in penalties takes effect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Gan shared his concerns about the safety of Police officers deployed at roadblocks and asked how many motorists at these roadblocks were detected for driving under the influence or having illegally modified vehicles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On driving under the influence, SPF detected an average of 700 cases per year from 2018 to 2020.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On illegally modified vehicles, LTA does not have a breakdown of the number of cases detected at roadblocks, as they do not conduct roadblocks per se.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Gan also asked if SPF would look into introducing barriers made of hardier material to minimise the risk to Police officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The safety of our Police officers is of paramount importance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For this reason, Police officers deployed to roadblock operations are equipped with reflective vests and traffic wands.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Emergency light beacons are also set up in the area to ensure they are highly visible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We also train our Police officers to react to situations where errant motorists might endanger the officers' safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Our officers will take into consideration factors such as prevailing traffic conditions and perform risk assessments when conducting roadblock operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On Mr Gan's suggestion to use hardier barriers, SPF will continue to review its procedures and processes to carry out roadblock operations in a safe and effective manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Gan also suggested that Auxiliary Police Officers, or APOs, can help to support SPF's roadblock operations, to better detect motorists who speed or drive in illegally modified vehicles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Currently, the SPF only deploys Police officers to roadblock operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Roadblock operations are inherently riskier, as officers may come across crimes such as possession of weapons or drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Hence, it requires Police officers who have undergone the appropriate training to handle such serious cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, Ms Sylvia Lim asked about the new offence which targets pedestrians near barriers in section 26 of the PFA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We would like to clarify that this provision is not meant to target pedestrians in relation to a roadblock.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Rather, section 26(7) targets members of the public who fail to proceed and stop before reaching barriers or cordons meant to control human traffic and remain there until permitted to continue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This refers to cordons that are used to ensure the safety of bystanders or control human traffic near crime scenes or high security areas, rather than roadblocks for motorists.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, on providing Police officers with the power to make forced entry in medical emergencies – a number of Members brought this up.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Sharael Taha raised questions regarding what constitutes a medical emergency and how Police officers assess a medical emergency behind locked doors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Dr Shahira Abdullah also suggested having clear guidelines on when Police officers should reasonably suspect that a medical emergency has taken place, before making forced entry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 7 of the Bill makes clear that a Police officer can make forced entry when he reasonably suspects that a person requires assistance because of any injury or poor state of health; that he is unable to enter the place; and is of the view that entry is necessary to protect the person's life, health or safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This allows Police officers to make forced entry for a variety of medical emergencies, ranging from a stroke to a serious fall.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Given that each case of medical emergency is unique and time-sensitive, instead of having prescriptive conditions, Police officers will take into consideration a variety of factors before making forced entry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, they look out for signs of distress such as audible shouts for help and seek more information from next-of-kin and neighbours to get a clearer picture of the situation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Louis Ng and Dr Shahira asked if Police officers already receive training to equip them with the skills needed to attend to medical emergencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Police officers are also instructed to immediately activate SCDF's emergency medical services where necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In cases where Police officers make forced entry and it turns out to be unwarranted, Dr Shahira asked if there would be proper recourse for the owner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There may, indeed, be instances when SPF will provide compensation for damage to property.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, such situations will be assessed on a case-by-case basis and will depend on the facts and circumstances of the case.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Dr Shahira also spoke on whether Police officers should make forced entry in cases of attempted suicide and asked if these officers are given protection.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We would like to clarify that Police officers already have the power to make forced entry for attempted suicide under sections 26A and 26B of the PFA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We share Dr Shahira's concern that such cases are highly complex.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For this reason, SPF has officers who are specially trained to intervene in attempted suicide cases, to prevent harm and prevent the loss of life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Where necessary, the Crisis Negotiation Unit will be activated to render assistance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Moving on, I will address Members' questions on according SPOs and CAOs with more necessary powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked why we are providing CAOs with full policing powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked if CAOs will be deemed as Police officers and be armed, given that the Bill accords CAOs with more policing powers which come with additional risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Yong also asked about the number of CAOs in SPF and the attrition rate for new CAOs and suggested deploying Police officers in the Commercial Affairs Department to supplement CAOs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Before I answer Ms Lim's and Mr Yong's questions, I would like to clarify that we are not providing CAOs with full policing powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While CAOs will be given more powers of arrest, search and other administrative powers, they will not be given powers not relevant to their work, such as the power to seize offensive weapons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To elaborate on why we are according CAOs with more powers, I would like to provide a backdrop of our crime trend.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In recent years, commercial and financial crimes have increasingly become an area of concern.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Not only has there been an uptick in such crimes, they have also become more complex in nature.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Therefore, it is necessary to equip our CAOs with more powers that are required to perform their duties, to enhance their operational efficiency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Having both CAOs and regular Police officers in CAD better allows us to bring perpetrators of white-collar crime to justice, as SPF can leverage on CAOs' specialised knowledge in the areas of accounting and finance while tapping on the broader investigation skills that regular Police officers have acquired from investigating into a wide range of crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Given that CAOs have the mandate to deal with white-collar crimes that are typically not violent or confrontational in nature, we assess that there is currently no operational need to deem them as full-fledged Police officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Hence, we will not be providing them with arms or with the full suite of policing powers, as I earlier mentioned.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Furthermore, should the Commercial Affairs Department encounter the need to use a higher level of force, they can leverage on regular Police officers in the Commercial Affairs Department who work alongside CAOs, as Mr Melvin Yong has suggested.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Yong also asked if CAOs will be required to undergo physical tests such as the Individual Physical Proficiency Test (IPPT) and be of a minimum Physical Employment Standard (PES), to exercise their new powers of arrest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We would like to clarify that the power of arrest is not new to CAOs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, they already have the power to arrest suspects of an arrestable offence under the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This Bill provides them with more powers of arrest which are relevant in their work, such as to arrest a person reasonably suspected to possess something which is fraudulently obtained.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In any case, I would like to assure Mr Yong that CAOs are required to undergo rigorous training and tests on safely conducting arrests and self-defence before they are allowed to exercise this power on the frontline.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We would also like to share that this approach is consistent with other non-uniformed officers who already have similar powers to investigate white-collar crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, authorised IRAS officers, whose core duty is to investigate tax crimes, are empowered to arrest suspects of serious tax crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if there will be safeguards and training for SPOs and CAOs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The SPF has multiple safeguards in place to ensure SPOs and CAOs exercise their new powers safely and in accordance with the law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, SPOs and CAOs will have to undergo modules on legal knowledge, self-defence and scenario-based training before they are deployed to the frontline.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, SPOs and CAOs will be subject to similar safeguards which Police officers are already subject to, such as those under the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, when SPOs and CAOs arrest a suspect, the suspect must not be restrained more than is necessary to prevent his escape, in accordance with section 76 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
